ROOTING BEYOND EARTH: ENHANCING BASIL CULTIVATION IN MARTIAN 
REGOLITH USING BIOFERTILIZERS AND ORGANIC AMENDMENTS 
 
ABSTRACT 
 
This study investigates the feasibility of cultivating Ocimum basilicum (Basil) in Martian 
regolith simulant using organic amendments and biofertilizers, with a focus on developing 
sustainable agricultural systems for future Mars colonization. We evaluated the efficacy of 
Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza (VAM), Plant Growth-Promoting Bacteria (PGPB), and 
Trichoderma in enhancing plant growth and productivity in Martian regolith compared to Earth 
soil. Our results demonstrate that PGPB treatment significantly improved plant performance in 
Martian regolith, with notable enhancements in chlorophyll concentration, net photosynthetic 
rate, and leaf development. The application of organic amendments and biofertilizers mitigated 
the toxic effects of Martian regolith, enabling microbial activity and plant growth. This research 
highlights the potential of biofertilizers, particularly PGPB, in facilitating sustainable food 
production in extraterrestrial environments and contributes to the development of closed-loop 
life support systems for future Mars missions. The findings have implications for optimizing 
crop cultivation in space exploration and advancing the sustainability of human 
presence beyond Earth. 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The exploration of Mars has undergone significant advancements, transitioning from telescopic 
observations to in-situ investigations. However, establishing sustainable food systems for 
future Mars missions poses substantial challenges due to the Martian regolith's inherent 
limitations, including low nutrient content, high salinity, and toxicity (Chinnannan et al., 2024). 
The regolith's natural properties, such as scarce nutrient availability, phytotoxic elements, and 
inadequate water retention capacity, render it inhospitable for vegetation. 
 
Recent studies emphasize the importance of understanding plant adaptability and evaluating 
their nutritional attributes for sustained Mars missions. Basil (Ocimum basilicum), with its 
adaptability, nutritional, and medicinal properties, is an ideal candidate for future Mars colonies

and human space exploration. Its rapid growth and maturation make it an attractive crop for 
testing in Martian simulant. 
 
This study aims to evaluate the feasibility of growing basil in Martian regolith using organic 
amendments and biofertilizers, excluding chemical fertilizers. Organic amendments, such as 
compost and manure, can enhance soil structure, water retention, and microbial activity, while 
biofertilizers optimize nutrient availability through beneficial microorganisms (Singh et al., 
2024). By adopting a chemical-free approach, this study seeks to establish a sustainable and 
closed-loop system essential for long-term space colonization. 
 
Notably, there is a lack of research on growing crops in Martian regolith using purely organic 
methods. This study addresses this gap by investigating the impact of organic amendments and 
biofertilizers, including bacterial consortium, on basil growth and productivity in Martian 
regolith. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of commercially and 
pharmacologically viable foundations for cultivation on the Martian surface. 
 
THEORY 
 
Plant Nutrition and Soil Fertility 
Plants require a balanced supply of essential nutrients to support their growth, development, 
and reproduction. There are 18 plant nutrient elements, including 9 macronutrients (C, H, O, 
N, P, K, Ca, Mg, and S) and 9 micronutrients (Fe, Zn, Mn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, and Ni) (Uchida, 
2000). Each plant species has an optimum nutrient range and minimum requirement level, and 
excessive nutrient uptake can cause poor growth due to toxicity (Silva & Uchida, 2000). Soil 
fertility refers to the ability of soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, providing essential 
nutrients and favorable chemical, physical, and biological characteristics (Tang, 2025). 
Organic Amendments and Biofertilizers 
Organic amendments, such as vermicompost, press mud, coir pith, biodynamic manure, peat 
moss, and biochar, can improve soil fertility and support microbial activity (Liu et al., 2023). 
These amendments have been shown to increase total microbial biomass, bacterial biomass, 
fungal biomass, Gram-positive bacterial biomass, and Gram-negative bacterial biomass. 
Biofertilizers, such as NPK biofertilizers, containing bacteria that fix nitrogen, solubilize 
phosphorus, and mobilize potassium, can enhance plant growth and nutrient uptake (N.M,

2022) . Three different treatments were used in this study: Vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizae 
(VAM), Plant Growth-Promoting Bacteria (PGPB), and Trichoderma viride. 
 
Basil Plant Characteristics and Requirements 
Basil (Ocimum basilicum L.) is a medicinal plant and culinary herb that requires a warm 
climate and high temperature, with soil that is fertile and has a pH range of 6.5 to 8 (Khater et 
al., 2021). It needs at least 6 to 8 hours of sunlight daily for optimal growth (Indira & Rani, 
2024). Basil has high nutritional content with low caloric values and contains vitamins A, B6, 
and C, as well as carotene, calcium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, and iron. 
Martian Regolith 
Martian regolith presents significant limitations for plant growth due to its low nutrient content, 
high salinity, and absence of organic carbon, which is essential for microbial activity and plant 
development (Kasiviswanathan et al., 2022). The Martian regolith is characterized by high pH 
levels and the presence of toxic perchlorates, which pose additional challenges to plant growth. 
Organic matter and biotic activity are not found in Martian soil, making it essential to provide 
exogenous inputs of organic matter to support plant growth. 
Developing techniques to eliminate or reduce salt toxicity and increase the fertility of Martian 
regolith by including organic materials reused from solid waste composting processes from the 
human habitat is crucial (Fackrell & Schroeder, 2020). This study aims to investigate the 
potential of using organic amendments and biofertilizers to improve soil fertility and support 
microbial activity, thereby enhancing plant growth in Martian regolith simulant. By providing 
optimum temperature, humidity, and photosynthetically active photons and controlling biotic 
factors, this study will determine the change between stages of crop growth. 
 
HYPOTHESIS 
Effect of soil amendments: 
H0: The mars regolith and the soil additive mix do not affect the biomass growth, yield, 
chlorophyll pigments quality, metabolites content, and microbial activity. 
H1: The Mars regolith and the soil additive mix affect the biomass growth, yield, chlorophyll 
pigments quality, metabolites content, and microbial activity. 
Effect of biofertilizers microbes: 
H0: The biofertilizer concentration does not affect the biomass growth, yield, chlorophyll 
pigments quality, metabolites content, and microbial activity.

H1: The biofertilizer concentration affects the biomass growth, yield, chlorophyll pigments 
quality, metabolites content, and microbial activity. 
Interaction of soil mixture – biofertilizer microbes: 
 H0: The mars regolith and the soil additive mix in conjunction with the biofertilizer do not 
affect the biomass growth and the chlorophyll pigments quality. 
H1: The mars regolith and the soil additive mix in conjunction with the biofertilizer 
concentration affect the biomass growth and the chlorophyll pigments quality. 
 
MATERIALS AND METHODS 
 
The test crop chosen was Basil (Ocimum basilicum). This is the heirloom variety of Italian 
basil seeds bought from Namdeo Umaji Agritech Pvt Ltd, Maharashtra, India. 
 
Number of sets: 2 (SET 1 – Mars regolith, SET 2 – Earth soil). Initial samples were analysed 
in Mars Simulant and Earth Soil before proceeding with the experiment. Each set had 4 
treatments with 3 replications. The amendments added were kept constants for all the 
treatments by converting the Mars regolith into cultivable soil, and the beneficial 
microorganisms were given as treatments without adding any inorganic form of fertilizers to 
prove the survival of microbes and its efficacy in mars soil and plant growth. 
 
Amendments added in 50 % (200 g) such as vermicompost 53 g, coir pith 53 g, press mud 53 
g , biodynamic manure 4 g, sphagnum moss 35 g, biochar 2 g , and organic NPK (nitrogen 
fixing, phosphate solubilizing and potash mobilizing) bacterial suspension 10 ml each are 
identical for all the treatments. Trichoderma is a soil fungi which provides plant growth 
promotion and induced systemic resistance against pest and diseases. 
 
Treatment 1: Mars regolith 200 g + Amendments + Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza (VAM) 
Treatment 2: Mars regolith 200 g + Amendments + Plant Growth-Promoting bacteria (PGPB) 
Treatment 3: Mars regolith 200 g + Amendments + Trichoderma 
Treatment 4: Mars regolith 200 g + Amendments 
Treatment 4 was kept as the control without adding NPK bacteria or Trichoderma. The same 
treatments were followed for comparison with earth soil instead of mars regolith. 
 
Amendments

The amendments such as vermicompost, coir pith, press mud, biodynamic manure, sphagnum 
moss, and biochar used for the experiment were collected from the Agri Farm, VIT School of 
Agricultural Innovations and Advanced Learning (VAIAL), Vellore, India. NPK bacteria and 
PGPB were produced by us by inoculating mother culture collected from Tamilnadu 
Agricultural University (TNAU), Coimbatore, India and multiplied at the Research Lab, VIT 
School of Agricultural Innovations and Advanced Learning (VAIAL), Vellore Institute of 
Technology, Vellore, India. Biofertilizers used for treatments such as Trichoderma and VAM 
were collected from VAIAL Farm. 
Vermicompost: a nutrient-rich organic fertilizer produced by worms breaking down organic 
waste. It enhances plant growth by providing essential micronutrients, improving soil structure, 
and increasing water retention. Vermicompost also boosts soil biodiversity and promotes 
healthy microbial activity, leading to healthier plants. 
Coir Pith: a byproduct of coconut husk, is a natural, eco-friendly soil amendment. It improves 
soil structure, increases water retention, and enhances aeration, promoting healthy root growth. 
Coir pith also supports beneficial microbial activity and reduces soil erosion, making it an ideal 
component for potting mixes and garden soils. 
Press mud: a byproduct of sugarcane processing, is a nutrient-rich organic amendment. It 
enhances soil fertility and water-holding capacity and serves as a natural source of 
macronutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. 
Biodynamic manure: It is made from cow dung from a lactating cow of average 50-150 g 
dung per horn, which is fermented and buried in the soil for 6 months. It helps to stimulate root 
growth and increases germination and humus formation. The BD 500 - Combination Manure 
(Cow horn + Cow dung + Flower manure) has its Nitrogen, Potassium, Phosphorus, and 
organic carbon content at 1.6%, 1.1%, 2.5%, and 24.50%, respectively, which will increase on 
a period basis. It helps to increase the root growth and increase the germination 
Sphagnum moss: a natural and highly absorbent soil amendment that provides a habitat for 
beneficial microorganisms. 
Biochar: Biochar can help mitigate heavy metal contamination in soil. On Mars, the soil 
contains heavy metals like perchlorates. Biochar's unique properties allow it to adsorb and 
immobilize these contaminants, reducing their availability to plants and microorganisms. 
NPK Bacteria: this NPK fertilizer is the consortium of Azospirillum, Bacillus sp and Fraturia 
aurantia. These are nitrogen fixing, phosphorus solubilizing and potassium mobilizing 
bacteria. They convert atmospheric nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium into a form that can 
be used by plants, available to plants and promoting their growth.

Treatments 
VAM: VAM (Vesicular Arbuscular mycorrhizal) biofertilizers are beneficial fungi that form 
symbiotic relationships with plant roots. They enhance soil fertility, improve plant growth, and 
increase the amount of nutrients available in the soil to plants. VAM biofertilizers also help 
reduce heavy metal toxicity in soil by immobilizing them, making them less available to plants. 
VAM fungi can deliver up to 80% of plant P, 25% of plant N, 10% of plant K, 25% of plant 
Zn, and 60% of plant Cu. 
PGPB: it is a bacterial consortium of beneficial microorganisms such as Bacillus Subtilis, 
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, Pseudomonas fluorescence and Methylobacterium. It can help to 
mitigate stress and support plant growth in mars soil. It enhances plant growth by improving 
soil nutrient availability producing plant hormones and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) 
that stimulate root development and nutrient uptake, and by regulating the soil microbial 
community. 
Trichoderma: it is a genus of beneficial fungi that promotes plant growth and soil health. It 
is used as a biological control agent to control plant pathogens, pests, and diseases. 
Trichoderma species can also solubilize minerals, improve soil structure, and enhance nutrient 
uptake. It can stimulate plant defense mechanisms, increasing resistance to stress and disease. 
 
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN & MEASUREMENTS 
 
Shade-net setup 
The experiment was conducted under a controlled environment (shade net house) with 
dimensions of 7m×7m×7m, which is located at VIT School of Agricultural Innovations and 
Advanced Learning (VAIAL), Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, India. The 
environmental variables measured during the experiment were temperature, relative humidity, 
light intensity, and airflow. The temperature was measured using a thermometer, relative 
humidity by hygrometer, wind speed by anemometer, and light intensity using PAR 
(Photosynthetically Active Radiation meter). The covering material used for shade net is high-
density polyethylene (HDPE) covering net, which protects plants from harmful UV rays.

Table 1. Shade net house parameters 
 
 Planting set up 
The pots mixture (Mars regolith, soil, amendments and treatments) were mixed thoroughly and 
pot filled before sowing and were placed in an order on the table kept inside the shade net 
house. One table had Earth soil pots, and another table had Mars regolith pots. The mars 
regolith and amendments were added at the ratio of 1:1 in all the twelve pots. Then, for the 
earth soil, amendments were added at the ratio of 1:1 in all twelve pots. After setting up pots 
with amendments and treatments, 20 seeds in each pot were sown, and the irrigation was done 
manually with 100 ml of distilled water added using measuring cylinders. The experimental 
setup is shown in Figure 1. 
• MT1: Mars regolith 50%, organic amendments 50%, VAM. 
• MT2: Mars regolith 50%, organic amendments 50%, PGPB. 
• MT3: Mars regolith 50%, organic amendments 50%, Trichoderma. 
• M-Control: Mars regolith 50%, organic amendments 50%.

By considering both mars regolith and earth soil with organic amendments, biofertilizers, 
irrigated water as independent variables, it was decided to define dependent variables as 
germination %, plant height, number of leaves, leaf area, yield, biomass, soil pH, EC, 
Chlorophyll, root development, secondary metabolites and available nutrients. The crop 
duration was expected to be 45 days. The harvest was done on the 45th day after sowing. 
 
Fig. 2. Identified variables in the experimental design. 
 
Analysis 
The pH and EC were measured every week in the soil from initial (before sowing) to final 
(during harvest). The pH in mars and Earth's initial soil before adding amendments was 
measured using digital pH meter and EC was measured using Conductivity meter. To measure 
the pH level of the soil after sowing, pH strips that was included in the kit of participation, the 
measurement was performed on a weekly basis. For this study we established to quantify the 
growth of the basil by measuring the characteristics such as duration of each growth stage 
(germination %, cotyledon appearance, seedling, and vegetative period), the morphological 
parameters (number of leaves, plant height, shoot length, root length and leaf area), plant´s 
physiological study includes (biomass production, and chlorophyll concentrations), SPAD 
values to identify chlorophyll content to measure photosynthetic rate. By taking account of 
these characteristics, it was considered the measuring schedule as shown in Table 2.

The cotyledon sprout and the appearance of leaves were visually inspected, and germination 
percentage was calculated; the day of each event was recorded in the experiment’s database. 
Similarly, the number of leaves were visually inspected and manually counted on weekly basis. 
In the same period of measurement, the height of the basil plant was measured using a ruler 
and by taking as reference the base of the stem. Leaf area was calculated by measuring length 
and breadth of leaves using ruler. To measure relative chlorophyll content in the basil plant 
leaves, SPAD (Soil Plant Analysis Development) meter was used on the 4th, 6th, and 8th grow 
weeks. 
 
In the Mars regolith at the initial stage before sowing, macro nutrients, micronutrients, and 
heavy metals were analyzed. After harvesting the plant samples, four analyses were carried 
out, i.e., nutrient analysis, heavy metals analysis, microbiome- metagenomics analysis, GC-
MS (Gas Chromatography- Mass Spectrometry), and Plant growth hormone analysis. 
 
For GC-MS analysis, 100 mg samples from all the treatments of Earth and Mars plants were 
taken. The procedure followed was as per the standard protocol. Metagenomic analysis to 
characterize all the bacterial species present in the soil samples is initiated. Soil samples were 
dried under shade for 24 hours and packed. Metagenomic analysis is being carried out at the 
paid service of BioKart Pvt Limited, Bangalore, India. For plant growth hormone analysis, 100 
mg of plant sample of best treatment and control were analysed using the standard procedures. 
For Heavy metals, analysis was carried out in both soil samples of 50 g and plant samples of

100 mg of all treatments were given at National Agro Foundation, Chennai. The results are 
given in the report in the results and discussion part. 
 
 
 
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 
 
Initial chemical analysis was done on mars regolith simulant before adding amendments using 
LaMotte soil testing kit before the start of the growth period. The results as shown in Table 3 
revealed a alkaline pH of 8.4 and an electrical conductivity of 1.77 mS/cm, which indicates a 
high concentration of salts leads to salinity problems which hinder the plant growth. In mars 
Regolith, the amendments and microbial cultures added before sowing was found to decrease 
in the Ph range in the first week. then , the pH of all treatments remained neutral to slightly 
alkaline (7.5 – 8.0) during last weeks of crop growth as well. EC also decreased to 0.98 mS/cm 
at last week shows significant reduction in the salt level and suitable for plant growth.

Table 4 and Figure 4 represents that the significant decrease in the pH in mars regolith after 
addition of organic amendments and different biofertilizers as treatments. Form this it clearly 
depicts treatment with Trichoderma (T3) has more reduction in the pH range from 7.15 to 7.00 
in mars regolith and in the earth soil the pH decrease from 7.5 to 6.74, which indicates that it 
becomes neutral from slightly alkaline and make ideal for better plant growth. Trichoderma 
produces many hydrolytic enzymes and hormones in addition to inducing the hormones in the 
plants. The presence of this fungi and its biochemical effects would have contributed to the 
reduction in pH. Thus the Mars regolith would definitely require microbes like Trichoderma 
for making it vulnerable to support crop growth in Mars.

After planting seeds of basil, the experiment was conducted during an 8-week grow period to 
end on their harvesting on March 30th. The evolution of this growth period is exemplified by 
the timeline shown in Figure 3. for the first repetition of the Mars regolith (M) composition 
provided with the treatment T2. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fig. 5. Growth process of the first replica of M soil mix under T2 treatment 
 
On the harvest day, firstly each repetition was photographed and then, plant parameters like 
plant height, foliar area, leaf count, chlorophyll concentration were measured. Then to obtain 
fresh weight of the basil, plants are harvested manually separately according to the treatment 
wise and measured its final root and shoot length. Then the shoot part is separated from the 
root by giving a cut, harvested leaves were shade dried for 24 hrs and dehydrated for 24 hrs by 
using hot air oven wit a temperature of 40°C. finally the dehydrated basil leaves were weighted 
again to record their dried weight and biomass was calculated. Further the dried plant sample 
used for various analysis.

The number of leaves had a similar development for the Basil plants of Mars regolith except 
control without influence of soil mix but the influence of treatments. In the Earth soil, all the 
treatments except control shows similar leaf count with influence of treatments given. This 
inference is made based on the analysis of both average number of leaves counted during 
harvest. In the case of leaf area, it had a significant development among different repetitions 
for each soil and treatment proposed for this experiment. Among the treatments in Mars 
regolith, second treatment (MT2) with PGPB shows a greater leaf area of 6.9 cm square 
followed by third treatment (MT3) with leaf area of 6.6 cm square. Similarly in Earth soil, ET2 
has greater leaf area of 10.5 cm square followed by ET1 with 10.0 cm square. The plant growth 
promoting bacteria produce hormones lie IAA and also induce the production of IAA in plants. 
The observed growth parameters including plant height and leaf area could be attributed to the 
growth promoting effects of the plant growth promoting bacteria. Hence, plant growth 
promoting bacteria are essential treatments required to grow plants in the Mars soil.

The above-mentioned table and figure depict the net photosynthetic rate of leaves in each 
treatment measured in both Mars regolith and Earth soil. Among Mars soil treatments, MT2 
with PGPB showed higher and positive NPR which indicates higher photosynthetic rate by 
absorbing more CO2 and converting into sugars for higher productivity, followed by treatments 
MT1 and MT3. The treatment with biofertilizers reduced the heavy metals concentration and 
improved the photosynthetic rate. The treatment with Control in Mars regolith showed in 
negative range which indicates the lower NPR and reduced productivity due to effects toxic 
metals in Martian regolith. Moreover, it also indicates the essential role of microorganisms 
(either PGPB or Trichoderma) in improving the photosynthesis of plants. Among the Earth soil 
treatments, all the treatments had positive and higher NPR in which treatment 2 with PGPB 
showed greater rate than others. This could be attributed to the already existing nutrients and 
microorganisms in Earth soil that even in pots without additional microbes, the net 
photosynthetic rate is on par with other treatments. The greater rate in PGPB treatment is an 
evidence to our hyphothesis that addition of mass multiplied plant growth promoting microbes 
are needed to supplement the native microbes in Earth soil for plant growth promotion and 
higher performance of the plants. If such is the case in Earth soil, microorganisms for plant 
growth promotion and photosynthetic activity in Mars soil is indispensable.

With the objective of checking the difference in the elements including micronutrients, trace 
elements and heavy metals in the Basil plants between treatments and control in Mars and Earth 
soil, elemental analysis was performed. The results are presented in Table 12 which indicated 
that there is either reduction or increase in the micronutrients and trace elements such as 
magnesium, sodium, copper, zinc etc. In the treatments with plant growth promoting bacteria, 
the micronutrients and trace element contents in the Basil plants increased indicating the role 
of bacteria in supplying these nutrients from the organic amendments added to the soils. 
However, heavy metals such as cadmium, chromium and nickel were below detectable 
quantities in both control and treatments. This indicates that although heavy metals were 
present in the Mars soil, the plants are not absorbing. This might be due to the effect of the soil 
amendments such as biodynamic manure, biochar etc added in the initial stage. 
 
Metabolic analysis of Basil plants using GC-MS 
 
Basil's phytochemical profile is characterized by the presence of rosmarinic acid, a dominant 
phenolic compound found in both leaves and stems, and eugenol, a phenolic compound with 
diverse health-promoting properties. These compounds contribute to basil's antioxidant, anti-
inflammatory, and antimicrobial activities, highlighting its potential health benefits 
and culinary value. The bioactive compounds were analysed only in the plants grown in 
Martian regolith.

Figure 12. GC – MS Spectrum for bioactive compounds in sample 1(MT1) 
GC-MS analysis identified several key compounds in basil. Eugenol, a phenolic compound 
with a molecular weight of 164.2 g/mol, was most abundant at a retention time of m/z = 17.66 
in Treatment 1 (MT1) with VAM. Rosmarinic acid, an organic acid with a molecular weight of 
360.32 g/mol, was most abundant at a retention time of m/z = 26.68. Additionally, glucose, a 
carbohydrate with a molecular weight of 180.156 g/mol, was detected at a retention time of 
17.52. These findings highlight the presence of bioactive compounds in basil with potential 
health benefits.

Fig. 13. GC – MS chromatogram for bioactive compounds in sample 2 (MT2) 
In this spectrum, Eugenol, a phenolic compound with a molecular weight of 164.2 g/mol, was 
most abundant at a retention time of m/z = 17.58 in Treatment 2 (MT2) with PGPB. Rosmarinic 
acid, an organic acid with a molecular weight of 360.32 g/mol, was most abundant at a retention 
time of m/z = 17.68. Additionally, Glucose with a molecular weight of 180.156 g/mol was 
detected at a retention time of 26.31. then another phenolic compound, caffeic acid, with a 
molecular weight of 180.16 g/mol at a retention time of 5.85. These findings highlight the 
presence of bioactive compounds in basil with potential health benefits.

Fig. 14. GC – MS chromatogram for bioactive compounds in sample 3 (MT3) 
In this spectrum, Eugenol, a phenolic compound with a molecular weight of 164.2 g/mol, was 
most abundant at a retention time of m/z = 17.56 in Treatment 3 (MT3) with Trichoderma 
viride. Rosmarinic acid, an organic acid with a molecular weight of 360.32 g/mol, was most 
abundant at a retention time of m/z = 15.90. Additionally, glutamic acid, a non-amino acid with 
a molecular weight of 180.156 g/mol, was detected at a retention time of 147.13. These findings 
highlight the presence of bioactive compounds in basil with potential health benefits.

Fig.15. GC – MS chromatogram for bioactive compounds in sample 4 (M - Control) 
In this spectrum, only eugenol is present with a molecular weight of 164.2 g/mol, and it was 
most abundant at a retention time of m/z = 17.58 in M-Control without any treatments. 
 
GC-MS analysis of plant samples grown in Martian soil revealed that Treatment 2 with Plant 
Growth-Promoting Bacteria (PGPB) exhibited a more diverse and complex chromatogram, 
indicating the presence of a greater number of bioactive compounds and secondary metabolites. 
This suggests that PGPB treatment may enhance the production of beneficial phytochemicals 
in plants grown in Martian soil. Hence, even if Basil is grown in Mars regolith, the amendments 
and treatments can help the plants not only grow well but also with same bioactive potential as 
like the plant’s growth in Earth soil.

CONCLUSION 
 
This study demonstrates the potential for growing basil in Martian regolith, a crucial step 
towards sustainable food production in space exploration. By comparing basil growth in 
Martian regolith to Earth soil and utilizing biofertilizers such as VAM, PGPB, and 
Trichoderma, with identical organic amendments across treatments, we identified the most 
effective approach for optimizing basil cultivation in Martian conditions. Our results clearly 
indicate that the application of PGPB with a bacterial consortium (Treatment 2) yielded 
superior outcomes across all evaluated growth parameters, including phenological and 
physiological attributes, secondary metabolite content, photosynthetic rate, and transpiration 
rate. These findings suggest that PGPB's plant growth-promoting properties can significantly 
enhance basil's adaptability and productivity in the challenging Martian regolith environment. 
 
The successful cultivation of Basil in Martian regolith, particularly with the enhanced 
performance observed under PGPB treatment, opens new avenues for utilizing this crop for 
both medicinal and culinary purposes in space missions. Basil's versatility and nutritional value 
make it an excellent candidate for contributing to the health and well-being of astronauts, while 
also providing fresh produce that can enhance the quality of life during long-duration space 
flights. 
 
In conclusion, this research not only advances our understanding of plant growth in 
extraterrestrial environments but also underscores the importance of biofertilizers in improving 
crop resilience and productivity. The insights gained from this study can inform future
